## python/carnot/verify/drift_probe.py

**Verdict:** `DISHONEST_NAMING`

## VERDICT
DISHONEST_NAMING

## CLAIMS

- Attributes to arXiv 2604.13386: “probing adjacent transformer layer pairs (L, L+1) captures a drift signal invisible to single-layer probes.”
- “The DRIFT paper reports that late layers exhibit the largest drift gap between truthful and hallucinating completions”
- “At inference time, return a calibrated violation probability.”
- Describes `model_runner` as executing “the LLM forward pass”.

## IMPLEMENTATION_REALITY
NumPy computes token-averaged cosine distances between supplied layer representations; scikit-learn genuinely fits and invokes `LogisticRegression`. LLM extraction is delegated to `model_runner`, with no bundled LLM invocation or explicit probability-calibration procedure.

## CLAIM_VS_REALITY_GAP
UNDISCLOSED_PROXY

## GAMING_PATTERNS
none — clipping bounds cosine-distance features to their mathematical range; `random_state=42` does not generate random features.

## RECOMMENDATION
RENAME_TO_REFLECT_REALITY

## RATIONALE
The cited [ensembling paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.13386v1#S3.SS4) combines independently trained layer-probe scores, while [DRIFT](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.14210v2#S3) uses an MLP or transformer on a single intermediate layer; neither establishes the adjacent-layer cosine-distance method attributed to them here. Delegated extraction is explicitly disclosed, but the methodological substitution is not, and a direct execution check also disproved the promised missing-runner fallback: training with nine correct examples and one hallucinated example returned approximately 0.10, not 0.5.

Live-model performance and calibration were not checked; exclude this verifier from headline AUROC until its attribution and fallback behavior are corrected.


## python/carnot/verify/drift_probe_ensemble.py

**Verdict:** `DISHONEST_NAMING`

## VERDICT
DISHONEST_NAMING

## CLAIMS

> “arXiv 2604.13386 shows that training one logistic regression probe per adjacent layer pair, then combining predictions via learned weighting (alpha), outperforms a single probe trained on the concatenated multi-layer drift vector by 3-8% AUROC.”

> “model_runner: Callable[[str], dict[int, np.ndarray]] — runs the LLM forward pass.”

> “The alpha weights are learned via grid search over a 20-point simplex”

## IMPLEMENTATION_REALITY
NumPy computes adjacent-layer cosine-distance scalars, and actual scikit-learn logistic regressions learn from those features; LLM execution is delegated to an injected callable, with no built-in model backend. Ensemble weights maximize validation accuracy over normalized random candidates, not a simplex grid.

## CLAIM_VS_REALITY_GAP
UNDISCLOSED_PROXY

## GAMING_PATTERNS
none — randomness selects splits and candidate weights, not fabricated classifier features; clipping probabilities to [0, 1] does not dodge perfect scores.

## RECOMMENDATION
RENAME_TO_REFLECT_REALITY

## RATIONALE
The cited paper probes standardized residual activations directly, using AUROC-tuned mixing for two layers and logistic-regression stacking for larger ensembles; it does not establish the claimed adjacent-drift-versus-concatenation result ([paper, §§3.2–3.4](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.13386)). The implementation contains real learning, but falsely attributes its materially different method to that paper without disclosing the substitution; exclude it from headline AUROC until its claims are corrected and independently validated.

Live inference was not checked; missing or failed runners silently become zero features and can produce valid-looking probabilities.
